title: Brazil’s women hold decisive votes in a presidential election too close to call
subtitle: Women make up almost 53% of Brazil’s electorate. As Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro contest a tightly balanced runoff, their choices could determine who governs—and whose promises on money, work and safety become policy.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Brazil’s presidential election reaches its decisive round on 25 October with no clear polling favourite and more than 83 million women eligible to help settle the contest between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

The Superior Electoral Court puts women at 52.84% of registered voters. In a race this close, their turnout and the choices of those still unconvinced by either candidate could determine the result. But the figures reveal a divided electorate, not a single ‘women’s vote’ waiting to be claimed.

A Quaest survey released on 24 October put Bolsonaro at 51% and Lula at 49% of valid voting intentions, within its two-percentage-point margin of error. Commissioned by TV Globo, it interviewed 3,702 voters in person on 23 and 24 October. Those estimates exclude blank and invalid votes; they are a measure of intention, not a result.
A gender gap with no guaranteed winner

Datafolha’s survey released on 22 October showed why both campaigns have reason to concentrate on women. Lula held 53% of valid voting intentions among female respondents against Bolsonaro’s 47%. Among men, Bolsonaro led by 54% to 46%.

That survey interviewed 2,520 voters in 154 municipalities between 20 and 22 October. Its national margin of error was two percentage points, rising to three points for the gender groups. Lula’s six-point advantage among women therefore sat at the boundary of that reported uncertainty.

The same poll found substantial differences by religion and income: Bolsonaro was stronger among evangelical voters, while Lula led among Catholics and people in households earning up to two minimum wages. These categories overlap. They cannot establish how every evangelical woman, low-income mother or young voter intends to vote.

For Lula, support among women offers a route to overcoming Bolsonaro’s strength elsewhere. For Bolsonaro, reducing his deficit among women could be enough. Neither calculation guarantees that people expressing a preference will reach the polling station.
The price of an ordinary day

The campaign has unfolded against frustration over living costs and household debt, despite improvements in unemployment and inequality, Reuters reported. Bolsonaro entered the runoff after taking roughly 47% in the first round, against Lula’s 45%.

Those economic pressures give the contest a practical dimension beyond political loyalty. A promise to improve family life must eventually be measured against wages, food bills, transport and the time available for paid work and care.

The Associated Press reported that Lula’s late campaign push included government support for small-business debt relief and a promise of free public transport at weekends. Bolsonaro has pledged lower food costs and made a tougher approach to crime central to his campaign.

These are different offers to voters confronting overlapping problems. Their value depends on implementation, eligibility and funding—details that matter more to a household budget than the force of a campaign slogan.
Being courted is not the same as being heard

Both candidates have explicitly sought women’s support. In a September analysis, Americas Quarterly described Bolsonaro’s proposals for financial-literacy courses, credit for women entrepreneurs and an artificial-intelligence assistant to receive domestic-violence reports. It also reported Lula’s pledge to introduce gender-equality lessons in schools.
The same analysis examined a Bolsonaro television advertisement featuring his wife, daughters and mother, presenting family relationships as evidence of his character.

Such appeals deserve scrutiny beyond their imagery. A reporting assistant would need a reliable connection to people able to respond to danger. Credit schemes would need affordable terms and realistic access. Classroom proposals would require trained teachers and sustained resources. Announcing a measure establishes an intention; it does not demonstrate an effective service.

Women’s electoral importance also sits alongside their limited access to candidacy. An August analysis by UOL, using electoral-court records, found women accounted for 34.8% of registered candidates across that year’s contests.

Political scientist Malu Gatto told UOL that parties often treated the minimum gender requirement as a ceiling. Electoral-law specialist Gabriela Rollemberg identified insufficient or late campaign funding as another obstacle. The imbalance begins before voters choose: parties influence who can afford to compete.
Today’s election can establish which candidate has secured enough support to govern. It cannot, by itself, show that either has earned lasting trust from women.

That judgement will be made through what follows: whether promised assistance reaches people, whether safety measures produce a response when help is requested, and whether women gain a stronger voice in decisions as well as a prominent place in campaign calculations.
The Athena Perspective.
